  3. The brick is deteriorating from sunlight, so it must be coated with a protective sealer on all of its faces
  4. The salts come only from the cleaning product used on the wall, so no investigation of the wall is needed
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Efflorescence forms when water dissolves soluble salts and carries them to the surface, where the water evaporates and leaves the salts behind. It is not mold and does not damage the material by itself. It is a signal that water is passing through the wall. Washing removes the deposit but it returns if the water source remains.

Concept Tested: Efflorescence

See: Efflorescence

docs.title: 17. Why is air-entrained concrete the standard defense against freeze-thaw damage for exterior concrete in cold climates?
docs.text:
1. Microscopic bubbles give freezing water, which expands about 9 percent, room to expand without cracking the concrete
  2. Microscopic bubbles stop all water from ever entering the concrete, so that freezing never occurs inside it
  3. Microscopic bubbles increase the compressive strength of the concrete to well above 10,000 psi in all cases
  4. Microscopic bubbles make deicing salts harmless, so the salts can be used freely on young concrete surfaces
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Freeze-thaw damage is the cracking, flaking, and crumbling of porous materials such as concrete, brick, and stone caused by water freezing inside them. It appears as spalling and as scaling, which deicing salts make worse. A low water-to-cement ratio also makes concrete less permeable, brick is selected for freeze-thaw resistance, and flashings, copings, and drainage keep water out of masonry.

Concept Tested: Freeze-Thaw Damage

See: Freeze-Thaw Damage

docs.title: 18. After a fire, a steel beam looks sound and unwarped. What should happen before the building is reoccupied?
docs.text:
1. The beam should be accepted as sound, because steel is a noncombustible material that cannot be harmed by heat
  2. A structural engineer should assess every damaged member, because a member can look sound yet have lost strength
  3. The beam should be painted and reoccupied, because the damage from the fire is only cosmetic in appearance
  4. The beam should be tested only if it is wood, because only wood chars and loses section in a fire
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Fire damage is the harm done by heat, flame, smoke, and the water used to extinguish a fire. Steel loses roughly half its strength near 1,100°F, concrete loses strength and may spall, and wood chars on the surface while the core remains sound. Smoke and soot spread beyond the burned area, and firefighting water often causes more widespread damage than the flames. Repairs trigger permits and inspections.

Concept Tested: Fire Damage

See: Fire Damage

docs.title: 19. Why does converting a warehouse into apartments often trigger major code upgrades?
docs.text:
1. A new use never changes the code requirements, because the building already exists and was previously approved
  2. A new use removes the need for a certificate of occupancy, because the structure has already been inspected
  3. A new use changes the occupancy classification, bringing new requirements for fire separations, egress, and sprinklers
  4. A new use applies only to the roof and has no effect on any of the other parts of the building
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Adaptive reuse is the conversion of an existing building to a use other than the one for which it was built, such as a flour mill that becomes housing or a museum. It saves the embodied carbon of the existing structure, preserves a community's character, and may qualify for historic preservation incentives. A feasibility study tests the structure, the code path, and the cost before the owner commits.

Concept Tested: Adaptive Reuse

See: Adaptive Reuse

docs.title: 20. How does deconstruction differ from demolition, and what makes it competitive?
docs.text:
1. Fast, mechanical destruction of the building so the debris can be hauled away, competing through lower labor cost
  2. Conversion of a building to a new use while keeping the structure, competing through historic preservation incentives
  3. Installation of new systems in an existing building to improve its performance, competing through energy savings
  4. Careful, selective dismantling to recover materials for reuse, competing through avoided disposal costs and resale value
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Deconstruction proceeds in roughly the reverse order of construction, with crews removing fixtures, doors, windows, flooring, and structural timber and sorting them for resale, donation, or recycling. It takes more labor than demolition and needs a hazardous-material survey before work. It works best when a building was designed for it, with mechanical fasteners and accessible connections, which is why designers who think about reuse at the start make it easier.

Concept Tested: Deconstruction

See: Deconstruction

Students will gain a broad understanding of the science and engineering principles that govern building construction

docs.text: Course Description

docs.title: Learning Graph for The Science of the Built Environment
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement Vew the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 6 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: The 380 concepts are grouped into 12 categories. No category exceeds 30% of the concepts.

docs.text: Checked on 2026-10-03. Of the 380 glossary entries, 111 contain numbers. Each number was checked in one of three ways: against a cited source, by arithmetic, or flagged as an illustrative value that no source supports.

docs.title: Corrections Made
docs.text: Glossary term Original claim Finding Source Snow Loads Minnesota ground snow 40 to 60 psf Minnesota uses 50 psf in most counties and 60 psf in 29 northern counties. Roof load is 0.7 × ground load. Minnesota DLI snow load map (Rules 1303.1700) Snow Loads 50 psf is "about 3 ft of fresh snow" Unsupported. Replaced with the 0.7 roof-load factor example. Same map Frost Depth "42 in. or more"; 60 in. "in some areas" Without an engineer's determination, minimum footing depth is 5 ft in Zone I (northern counties) and 3.5 ft (42 in.) in Zone II. Minnesota Rules 1303.1600 (UpCodes), Revisor version Allowable Building Area Wood-frame store limited to 12,500 sq ft Not in IBC Table 506.2. Group M, Type VB is 9,000 sq ft unsprinklered (Type VA is 14,000). IBC 2018 Chapter 5, Minnesota edition (UpCodes) Soil Bearing Capacity Firm clay about 2,000 psf The IBC presumptive value for clay, sandy clay, silty clay, clayey silt, silt and sandy silt is 1,500 psf. The spread-footing example was recalculated. IBC Table 1806.2 (UpCodes) Local Materials Benchmark of 500 miles 500 miles was the older LEED benchmark. LEED v4 uses 100 miles. GBRI: LEED v4 regional materials National Electrical Code Minnesota adopts it "with amendments" Minnesota Rules chapter 1315 adopts NFPA 70 by reference. The sources found did not show state amendments, so the claim was removed. Minnesota Rules ch. 1315 Rot and Decay Needs moisture above about 20% Decay generally needs wood above about 25 to 30% (near fiber saturation). Below 20% is a common protective limit, not the decay threshold. USDA Wood Handbook, Chapter 14 Live Loads 40 psf for residential floors 40 psf applies to most areas of one- and two-family dwellings. Sleeping rooms and habitable attics are 30 psf. IBC 2018 Chapter 16, Minnesota edition (UpCodes) Fiberglass Insulation R-19 batts fit between 2x6 ceiling joists A 2x6 is 5.5 in. deep, so R-19 (about 6.25 in.) would be compressed. Replaced with R-13 batts in 2x4 walls. PS 20 lumber sizes (NIST) Low-Voltage Systems "50 volts or less" NEC Article 720 says less than 50 volts. Note that Article 720 was removed from the 2023 NEC. docs.title: Interactive Infographic Posters
docs.text:
These posters turn the book's biggest systems ideas into visual, classroom-ready learning experiences. Open a poster, hover over or click a region to read what it shows, then switch to Quiz mode to test yourself.

The original concepts and their sources are in Infographic Poster Ideas.

  • The House as a System

    A house performs as one system in which the envelope, the mechanical systems, and the occupants together steer the flow of heat, air, and moisture. Callout overlay, 11 markers.

  • The Perfect Wall: Four Control Layers

    A wall must control rain, air, vapor, and heat, in that order of importance, and Lstiburek's Perfect Wall puts all four layers outside the structure. Callout overlay, 11 markers.

  • The Six S's of Shearing Layers

    A building is a stack of six layers that change at very different speeds, and good design lets the fast layers slip past the slow ones. Grid overlay, 6 regions.

  • Four Ways Moisture Moves

    Moisture reaches a building as bulk water, capillary action, air-carried vapor, and vapor diffusion, and air leakage and liquid water do far more damage than diffusion. Grid overlay, 5 regions.

  • Heat on the Move

    Heat moves by conduction, convection, and radiation, and thermal bridges let it bypass insulation, so insulation only works if heat cannot go around it. Grid overlay, 6 regions.

  • The Load Path

    Every load on a building needs a continuous, unbroken route to the ground, and a broken link anywhere along it lets something move. Callout overlay, 12 markers.

  • The Whole Building Design Wheel

    A good building balances eight design objectives, and an integrated approach and team process keep the balance around a high-performance building. Callout overlay, 12 markers.

  • The Five Principles of Passive House

    Passive House reaches very low energy use with five linked measures that work as a system, and skipping one weakens the rest. Callout overlay, 8 markers.

  • The Indoor Species

    People spend most of their lives inside buildings, so Harvard's nine foundations of a healthy building treat the building as a habitat. Grid overlay, 10 regions.

  • Thermal Comfort Is Six Variables

    Thermal comfort depends on four environmental and two personal variables, and the outdoor climate also shifts what people accept. Callout overlay, 11 markers.

  • The Carbon Footprint of the Built World

    Buildings are a leading climate lever, and the carbon in materials matters as much as the energy used to run them, but every share depends on where its source draws the boundary. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • Cradle to Grave to Cradle

    A building's carbon impact starts at the quarry and continues past demolition, and the life-cycle modules show which emissions are embodied and which are operational. Grid overlay, 9 regions.

  • The Building as a Chimney

    In winter every tall building is a chimney, and the same stack-effect physics that wastes heat and causes drafts can also carry smoke between floors. Callout overlay, 10 markers.

  • The Swiss Cheese Model of Building Failure

    Buildings rarely fail from a single cause; failure happens when holes in several layers of defense line up, and redundancy keeps them from aligning. Grid overlay, 8 regions.

  • The Living Building Petals

    The Living Building Challenge describes a regenerative building as seven connected performance areas, called petals, and asks it to give back more than it takes. Callout overlay, 10 markers.

  • Nature in the Room

    Terrapin Bright Green's patterns of biophilic design treat daylight, views, and natural materials as inputs to occupant well-being, not decoration. Callout overlay, 10 markers.

  • When the Power Goes Out

    Passive survivability asks a building to keep its occupants safe when the grid and the furnace fail, and six passive strategies do most of the work. Grid overlay, 9 regions.

  • Minnesota Asks Hard Questions

    Climate is the first design input, and each hard question a Minnesota winter and summer ask of a building has a matching cold-climate design answer. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • Idea to Occupancy

    A building is made by a sequence of phases, and the earlier a decision is made, the cheaper it is to get right. Grid overlay, 8 regions.

  • The Building Systems Map

    Every building system depends on every other, so a change to one must be followed through all the others. Callout overlay, 12 markers.

docs.title: Hours Saved Estimate
docs.text:
This page estimates how many human hours an artist, a graphic designer, and an instructional designer would have needed to create the 20 interactive infographic posters in this book. It is a judgment-based estimate built from typical production rates for each role. It is not measured.

The estimated total is about 790 specialist hours, or roughly 835 human hours if the instructor's time in the weekly meetings is counted. A reasonable range is 600 to 1,100 specialist hours. At typical market rates that is about $54,000 of specialist labor, within a range of roughly $21,000 to $107,000.

docs.title: Work by Role
docs.text: Role Work Hours Instructional designer Research and select the 20 frameworks, about 30 hours. Per poster (about 9 hours each): learning objectives, chapter alignment, 5 to 12 region descriptions with 3 to 5 facts each, 8 to 12 quiz questions, source checking, and the art brief. Review cycles, about 20 hours. ~230 Artist 20 detailed technical illustrations, each with a different composition and no reused scene. About 14 hours each: sketch, line work, color, revisions to match the brief, and a character cameo. ~280 Graphic designer Style system, palette, type and layout rules, about 20 hours. Per poster (about 4 hours): composition review and region layout. Overlay integration and calibration, about 30 hours. Thumbnails, export and QA, about 20 hours. ~150 Subtotal ~660

docs.title: Meetings
docs.text:
The three specialists would meet with the instructor 4 hours a week. The artist is the bottleneck. The designer and instructional designer work ahead of and alongside the artist, so the estimate assumes about 11 calendar weeks. That is roughly 7 weeks of artist production plus sequencing and review cycles.

Item Hours 3 specialists × 4 hours × 11 weeks ~132 Instructor's own time in those meetings (not specialist time) ~44

docs.title: Totals
docs.text: Hours Specialist hours (work plus meetings) ~790 Including instructor meeting time ~835

docs.title: What This Leaves Out
docs.text:
• Project management, licensing, and accessibility review.
  • Instructor review time outside the weekly meetings.
  • Extra concept rounds if the instructor changes direction mid-project.

The range goes up if the art has to be hand-drawn at the technical accuracy in the image prompts, with several revision rounds per poster. It goes down if the artist works from stock vector assets or the team reuses scenes across posters.

docs.title: Hourly Rates
docs.text:
Rates vary widely by source, seniority, and region, and none of these figures is specific to Minneapolis. The scenarios below use three rate levels for each role.

Role Low Typical High Basis Instructional designer $38 $70 $100 Low is the reported average freelance pay. Typical is an established freelancer. High is a senior specialist. Graphic designer $34 $65 $90 Low is the reported average employee or freelance wage. Typical is a mid-level designer. High is a senior designer. Artist (technical illustrator) $34 $70 $100 Low is the reported average technical illustrator wage. Typical is a mid-to-senior freelance illustrator. High is a senior illustrator.

The low rates are average wages, so they understate what a team would charge as contractors. The typical rates are the most realistic for a commissioned project. The rate ranges come from these sources:

docs.text:
Each role's hours are its work hours plus its 44 meeting hours (4 hours a week for about 11 weeks). The low and high scenarios scale every role's hours to the 600 and 1,100 totals.

Scenario Instructional designer Graphic designer Artist Total hours Total cost Low 207 h × $38 = $7,866 147 h × $34 = $4,998 245 h × $34 = $8,330 599 $21,194 Typical 274 h × $70 = $19,180 194 h × $65 = $12,610 324 h × $70 = $22,680 792 $54,470 High 381 h × $100 = $38,100 269 h × $90 = $24,210 450 h × $100 = $45,000 1,100 $107,310

  • It does not subtract the cost of the AI tools used, or the author's own time reviewing and revising the generated posters.
  • The instructor's 44 hours in meetings are not priced, because that is faculty time and not specialist time.
  • It does not include project management, licensing, or accessibility review.

docs.title: Infographic Poster Ideas
docs.text: This page proposes 20 infographic posters that give students a holistic, systems-level view of the science of the built environment. Each idea is grounded in a framework or diagram that has shaped how building professionals think, and each includes a detailed image description that an illustrator, an AI image generator, or a MicroSim author can work from.

docs.title: How This List Was Built
docs.text:
I searched for the diagrams and frameworks that practitioners, researchers, and standards bodies use to explain buildings as systems rather than as piles of parts. Two honest caveats:

  • No single canonical "holistic poster" exists. The field's most influential visuals are individual diagrams (the control layers, the shearing layers, the life-cycle stages) rather than one master poster. This list takes those diagrams and turns each into a full poster concept.
  • These are original designs, not reproductions. I worked from the published descriptions of each framework, not from copies of the artwork. Every poster below should be drawn fresh, and the source framework should be credited in the poster footer. Numeric claims should be re-checked against the cited source before a poster is finalized.

docs.title: Common Design Standards
docs.text:
Use these for every poster so the set reads as one family.

Element Standard Format Landscape, 16:9 (1920 × 1080 px for the web, 36 × 24 in for print) Palette Safety orange #FF6A13 for focal points, chestnut brown for structure, cream for backgrounds, slate blue for water and moisture, brick red for heat, sage green for sustainability Typography One bold sans-serif title, one clean sans-serif for labels, and a minimum 18 px label size at web resolution Footer Chapter links, the source framework credit, and the line "The Science of the Built Environment" Mascot Beau the Beaver may appear once per student-facing poster, in the pose that matches the job (thinking, warning, tip). Instructor-facing versions omit Beau. Accessibility Never use color alone to carry meaning; pair every color with a label, pattern, or icon

docs.title: The Top 20 at a Glance
docs.text:
# Poster Core idea Chapters 1 The House as a System Envelope, mechanical systems, and occupants all drive heat, air, and moisture flow 3, 4, 19 2 The Perfect Wall Four control layers, in priority order 11, 12 3 The Six S's of Shearing Layers Building layers change at different speeds 1, 21 4 Four Ways Moisture Moves Bulk water, capillarity, air, and vapor diffusion 4, 11, 21 5 Heat on the Move Conduction, convection, radiation, and thermal bridges 3, 19 6 The Load Path Every force finds its way to the ground 6, 7, 8, 10 7 The Whole Building Design Wheel Eight objectives balanced by one integrated team 2, 17 8 The Five Principles of Passive House Five measures that work only together 19 9 The Indoor Species We live indoors, so the building is our habitat 4, 14 10 Thermal Comfort Is Six Variables Four environmental and two personal factors 4 11 The Carbon Footprint of the Built World Operations versus embodied carbon 20 12 Cradle to Grave to Cradle Life-cycle stages A through D 20 13 The Building as a Chimney Stack effect links envelope, HVAC, and fire safety 4, 14, 18 14 The Swiss Cheese Model of Building Failure Failures need aligned holes in several defenses 17, 18, 21 15 The Living Building Petals Seven performance areas of a regenerative building 20 16 Nature in the Room Biophilic design patterns and occupant well-being 4, 16 17 When the Power Goes Out Passive survivability and resilience 19, 21 18 Minnesota Asks Hard Questions What a cold climate demands of every system 9, 10, 11, 13 19 Idea to Occupancy Who does what in each project phase 2, 16, 17 20 The Building Systems Map How every system depends on every other 14, 15, 16, 19

Posters 1, 2, 3, 7, and 20 are the most holistic. If only a few are produced, start there.

docs.title: Poster 1: The House as a System
docs.text:
Influence: The U.S. Department of Energy's Building America program treats the house as a system whose performance depends on a balance of the envelope, the mechanical systems, and the occupants. All three affect the flow of heat, air, and moisture into and out of the building.

Core message: A building is not a collection of products. Change one part and the whole system responds.

Chapters: 3, 4, 19

Image description:

  • Layout: A cutaway cross-section of a two-story Minnesota house sits in the center, filling about 60% of the canvas.
  • Three actors: Three large labeled rings overlap in a Venn arrangement behind the house: Envelope (chestnut), Mechanical Systems (slate blue), and Occupants (safety orange). The overlap zone behind the house reads "Building Performance."
  • Flows: Three families of arrows cross the house. Red arrows show heat flow, blue arrows show air flow, and teal droplet-arrows show moisture flow. Heat arrows leave through the walls, roof, and windows. Air arrows enter low (leaks at the sill) and exit high (leaks at the attic). Moisture arrows rise from the shower and kitchen.
  • Callouts: Each ring gets three short callouts. Envelope: insulation, air sealing, windows. Mechanical: furnace, ventilation, water heater. Occupants: thermostat setting, showers and cooking, windows opened.
  • Footer strip: "Heat. Air. Moisture. Three flows, one system."
  • Beau: Thinking pose, lower right, pointing at the overlap.

docs.title: Poster 2: The Perfect Wall
docs.text:
Influence: Joseph Lstiburek's "Perfect Wall" from Building Science Corporation (BSI-001). A wall must control rain, air, vapor, and heat. In order of importance the layers are the rain control layer, the air control layer, the vapor control layer, and the thermal control layer. Lstiburek's slogan is to keep the outside out, and the best place for the layers is outside the structure.

Core message: Control layers cascade in priority. If you cannot keep the rain out, do not worry about the air.

Chapters: 11, 12

Image description:

  • Layout: A horizontal wall cross-section runs left to right, from outdoors on the left to indoors on the right, drawn in layers like a stack of slices pulled slightly apart.
  • Layers, outside to inside: Cladding, drainage gap, water-resistive barrier, continuous exterior insulation, sheathing, studs, cavity, drywall.
  • Control layer overlay: Four colored bands run above the wall, each ending in a vertical bracket that marks where that control layer sits. Blue is rain, green is air, yellow is vapor, and red is thermal.
  • Priority ladder: On the right, a vertical ladder numbered 1 to 4 ranks the layers: Rain, Air, Vapor, Thermal. A bold note beside it reads "If layer 1 fails, layers 2 to 4 cannot save you."
  • Material callouts: A small inset shows that one material can serve several layers, such as a liquid-applied membrane that is both the water and air control layer.
  • Sun and snow icons on the exterior side; a warm living room silhouette on the interior side.
  • Beau: Tip pose, with a tape measure held against the thickness of the wall.

docs.title: Poster 3: The Six S's of Shearing Layers
docs.text:
Influence: Frank Duffy's layered model of building change, expanded by Stewart Brand in How Buildings Learn into six layers: Site, Structure, Skin, Services, Space Plan, and Stuff. The layers have very different lifespans, and an adaptable building lets them slip past one another.

Core message: A building is a stack of components on different clocks. Design so the fast layers can change without breaking the slow ones.

Chapters: 1, 21

Image description:

  • Layout: A large onion-style exploded diagram of one building, with six concentric or stacked layers peeled apart, from the outermost (Site) to the innermost (Stuff).
  • Per-layer content:
    • Site: the lot and soil, drawn as terrain with a property line. Lifespan label: "Eternal."
    • Structure: foundation and frame. Label: "30 to 300 years."
    • Skin: the exterior surfaces. Label: "About 20 years."
    • Services: wires, pipes, ducts. Label: "7 to 15 years."
    • Space Plan: interior walls and doors. Label: "3 to 30 years."
    • Stuff: furniture and belongings. Label: "Days to years."
  • Time ruler: A logarithmic ruler along the bottom, with each layer's lifespan drawn as a bar, from a short orange bar for Stuff to a very long chestnut bar for Structure.
  • Sidebar: "Slipping layers": two layers drawn with a dashed gap between them, versus two layers fused together with a crack running through them.
  • Beau: Thinking pose.

docs.title: Poster 4: Four Ways Moisture Moves
docs.text:
Influence: The DOE and Building Science Corporation moisture-physics literature identifies four transport mechanisms: bulk (liquid) water, capillary action, air-transported moisture, and vapor diffusion. Bulk water is the potentially most damaging mechanism, and air leakage typically moves far more water vapor than diffusion does.

Core message: Most people worry about diffusion. Air leakage and liquid water do most of the damage.

Chapters: 4, 11, 21

Image description:

  • Layout: A four-panel grid, each panel showing the same simple wall-and-foundation section with a different mechanism highlighted.
  • Panel A, Bulk water: Rain running down a wall and pooling at a foundation, with a roof leak and a flashing gap highlighted. Blue arrows.
  • Panel B, Capillary action: A concrete footing wicking groundwater upward into a wall, drawn with a magnified inset of tiny pores and rising water.
  • Panel C, Air-transported moisture: Warm humid indoor air streaming through an electrical outlet and a top-plate gap, condensing on cold sheathing. Wavy air arrows carrying small droplets.
  • Panel D, Vapor diffusion: Individual vapor molecules passing slowly through drywall, drawn as tiny dots drifting through a porous layer.
  • Ranking bar: A horizontal bar under the grid ranks relative damage potential, with the bar for air and bulk water drawn much longer than the bar for diffusion.
  • Beau: Warning pose beside Panel C, with the note "A one-inch hole beats a whole wall of vapor barrier."

docs.title: Poster 5: Heat on the Move
docs.text:
Influence: Foundational building-science heat-transfer teaching: conduction, convection, and radiation, and the way thermal bridges let heat bypass insulation. Passive House practice makes thermal-bridge-free detailing one of its core principles.

Core message: Insulation only works if heat cannot go around it.

Chapters: 3, 19

Image description:

  • Layout: Split canvas. The left half shows three heat-transfer modes; the right half shows an infrared-style thermal image of a wall.
  • Left half: Three small vignettes in a column. Conduction: a spoon in hot soup, then a stud conducting heat through a wall. Convection: air rising along a warm radiator and falling at a cold window. Radiation: a sun-warmed floor and a person feeling chill near a cold window.
  • Right half: A false-color thermal view of an exterior wall with warm stripes where studs and rim joists sit, labeled "Thermal bridges." Cooler colors show the insulated cavities.
  • Detail inset: A balcony slab penetrating the wall, with a heat "leak" arrow, versus the same detail with a thermal break.
  • Footer: "R-value is the label. Detailing is the result."
  • Beau: Tip pose with a flashlight, "Look for the studs in the frost."

docs.title: Poster 6: The Load Path
docs.text:
Influence: The structural-engineering principle that every load must have a continuous, unbroken path to the ground. This is a standard concept in structural education rather than a single published diagram.

Core message: Follow the force. Roof, wall, floor, foundation, soil. Break the path and something moves.

Chapters: 6, 7, 8, 10

Image description:

  • Layout: A tall wood-frame house section on the left with a bright orange arrow tracing the load from the roof to the soil.
  • Path steps: Numbered stations along the arrow: 1 Roof snow and wind, 2 Rafters and trusses, 3 Headers over openings, 4 Studs and posts, 5 Floor framing, 6 Foundation wall, 7 Footing, 8 Soil.
  • Load types: A color-coded key shows dead load, live load, snow load, wind load, and seismic load, with a small arrow icon for each. Wind is drawn pushing sideways and uplifting the roof.
  • Right panel: Three "what if" thumbnails: a removed bearing wall with a sagging floor, a missing hurricane tie with a roof lifting, and a footing on soft soil settling.
  • Comparison strip: Four miniature building types (wood, steel, concrete, masonry) each with its own load path drawn in orange.
  • Beau: Warning pose, "Check your load path!"

docs.title: Poster 7: The Whole Building Design Wheel
docs.text:
Influence: The National Institute of Building Sciences' Whole Building Design Guide (WBDG) diagram: a high-performance building at the center, wrapped by an Integrated Team Process and Integrated Design Approach, with eight design objectives around the outer ring: Accessible, Aesthetics, Cost-Effective, Functional/Operational, Historic Preservation, Productive, Secure/Safe, and Sustainable.

Core message: Good buildings balance competing objectives. The team that designs together builds better.

Chapters: 2, 17

Image description:

  • Layout: A large wheel. The center disc is a simple building icon labeled "High-Performance Building." A ring around it is labeled "Integrated Team Process" and "Integrated Design Approach."
  • Outer ring: Eight equal segments, one per objective, each with an icon: a wheelchair ramp, a facade, a dollar sign, a floor plan, a historic column, a person at a desk, a shield, and a leaf.
  • Spokes: Thin lines connect adjacent objectives, with small "tension" labels, such as a daylight window between Aesthetics and Sustainable, or a fire door between Secure/Safe and Accessible.
  • Team strip: Along the bottom, small portraits of the owner, architect, engineer, contractor, inspector, and electrical designer all pointing at the center.
  • Beau: Thinking pose.

docs.title: Poster 8: The Five Principles of Passive House
docs.text:
Influence: The Passive House standard's five principles: continuous super-insulation, airtight construction, high-performance windows and doors, thermal-bridge-free design, and balanced ventilation with heat recovery. Sources describe the approach as holistic and report heating and cooling energy reductions of up to about 90% compared with conventional construction.

Core message: Five measures, one outcome. Skip one and the others lose power.

Chapters: 19

Image description:

  • Layout: A cutaway of a compact two-story house, with five numbered orange tags attached to features.
  • Tags: 1 Insulation wraps the entire envelope, drawn as a thick continuous blanket. 2 A blower-door fan sits in the front doorway with a gauge, labeled airtightness test. 3 Triple-pane windows with a cross-section inset showing the glass layers. 4 A thermal-break detail where the wall meets the foundation. 5 A heat-recovery ventilator in the utility room, with two crossing airstreams swapping heat but not air.
  • Interdependence web: A five-pointed star in the corner connects all five principles with lines, labeled "Remove any point and the star collapses."
  • Result badge: "Up to about 90% less heating and cooling energy." Verify the claim against the current Passive House Institute figure before publishing.
  • Beau: Celebration pose, small, in the corner.

docs.title: Poster 9: The Indoor Species
docs.text:
Influence: The National Human Activity Pattern Survey (NHAPS), funded by the U.S. EPA and published by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in 2001, found that Americans spent about 86.9% of their time indoors, plus about 5.5% in vehicles, the origin of the often-quoted "90% indoors." The Harvard Healthy Buildings program adds the "9 Foundations of a Healthy Building."

Core message: Because we are an indoor species, the building is our primary environment, and it should be designed like a habitat.

Chapters: 4, 14

Image description:

  • Layout: The top third is a 24-hour clock ring colored by location: a large slice for home, work, and school, a small slice for vehicles, and a thin slice for outdoors.
  • Bottom two-thirds: A nine-tile grid, one tile per foundation, each with an icon: ventilation, air quality, thermal health, moisture, dust and pests, safety and security, water quality, noise, lighting and views.
  • Tile content: Each tile carries a one-line student-friendly "what it means" and a chapter link.
  • Source note: "NHAPS 1992 to 1994, U.S. EPA / LBNL." A small footnote points out that the 90% figure is an average of surveyed U.S. adults, not a universal constant.
  • Beau: Thinking pose, "Your building is your habitat."

docs.title: Poster 10: Thermal Comfort Is Six Variables
docs.text:
Influence: P. O. Fanger's Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) model, used in ASHRAE Standard 55, which combines environmental variables (air temperature, radiant temperature, air speed, humidity) with personal factors (clothing insulation and metabolic rate). Brager and de Dear's adaptive model adds that acceptable indoor temperatures also shift with the outdoor climate.

Core message: Comfort is not just the thermostat number.

Chapters: 4

Image description:

  • Layout: A central figure of a seated person, with six spokes radiating out to labeled icons.
  • Spokes: Air temperature (a thermometer), mean radiant temperature (a sun-warmed or cold wall), air speed (a draft), relative humidity (a droplet gauge), clothing insulation (a sweater), and metabolic rate (a person walking versus sitting).
  • Scale strip: A horizontal seven-point sensation scale along the bottom: Cold (-3), Cool (-2), Slightly cool (-1), Neutral (0), Slightly warm (+1), Warm (+2), Hot (+3).
  • Case studies: Three small scenes: a person next to a cold window with a 72 °F thermostat reading yet feeling chilly; a gym at the same temperature feeling too hot; a naturally ventilated room in summer where people accept a warmer range.
  • Beau: Tip pose, "The cold window beat the thermostat."

docs.title: Poster 11: The Carbon Footprint of the Built World
docs.text:
Influence: Architecture 2030's widely used chart of the built environment's share of global CO₂ emissions. Their published figures are about 42% of annual global CO₂ emissions: roughly 27% from building operations and roughly 15% from the embodied carbon of materials and construction. They also project about 2.6 trillion square feet (241 billion square meters) of new floor area from 2020 to 2060, "the equivalent of adding an entire New York City to the world, every month, for 40 years," and note that three-quarters of the infrastructure that will exist in 2050 has yet to be built. The UNEP Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2024/2025 gives a different accounting: 32% of global energy and 34% of CO₂ emissions.

Core message: Buildings are a leading climate lever, and materials matter as much as operating energy.

Chapters: 20

Image description:

  • Layout: A large donut chart on the left shows all human CO₂ emissions, with the building-related slice pulled out. The pulled-out slice splits into two labeled parts: Operational (about 27%) and Embodied (about 15%).
  • Right panel: A skyline silhouette made of stacked blocks. Each block is labeled with a material: cement, steel, aluminum, timber, glass, insulation.
  • Timeline bar: "2020 → 2060: 241 billion m² of new floor area" drawn as a long bar of repeating small city icons.
  • Accounting note: A small footnote explains that different sources draw the boundary differently, comparing the Architecture 2030 and UNEP figures side by side. Never mix the two in one number.
  • Beau: Warning pose, "Check which boundary the number uses."

docs.title: Poster 12: Cradle to Grave to Cradle
docs.text:
Influence: The life-cycle stage structure in EN 15978: A1 to A3 product stage, A4 to A5 transport and construction, B1 to B7 use stage, C1 to C4 end of life, and Module D for benefits beyond the system boundary. Embodied carbon covers modules A1 to A5, B1 to B5, and C1 to C4; operational carbon covers B6 and B7.

Core message: A material's impact does not start at the jobsite or end at the dumpster.

Chapters: 20

Image description:

  • Layout: A long horizontal timeline in the shape of a looping ribbon, with four colored stages in order.
  • Stage A, Product and Construction (A1 to A5): Quarry, factory, truck, crane. Highlight A1 to A3 as the "upfront carbon" burst.
  • Stage B, Use (B1 to B7): A building with a wrench, a paint roller, a replaced window, and a meter. B6 and B7 flagged as operational energy and water.
  • Stage C, End of Life (C1 to C4): Demolition, sorting, transport, landfill.
  • Module D, Beyond the boundary: A curved arrow looping from C back to A with icons for reuse and recycling.
  • Overlay bracket: Two brackets over the timeline: "Embodied carbon" and "Operational carbon."
  • Beau: Thinking pose.

docs.title: Poster 13: The Building as a Chimney
docs.text:
Influence: The stack effect, as treated in Building Science Corporation's BSI-075 and in fire-protection engineering. Warm indoor air rises and leaves high, drawing cold outdoor air in low. In a fire, stack effect can carry smoke and interfere with smoke-control systems.

Core message: In winter every tall building is a chimney, and the same physics that wastes heat can spread smoke.

Chapters: 4, 14, 18

Image description:

  • Layout: A tall multi-story building cross-section with an elevator shaft and stairwell highlighted as vertical "flues."
  • Airflow: Blue arrows enter low on the cold side and red arrows exit high near the roof. A dashed horizontal line marks the "neutral pressure plane" about halfway up, with pressure plus and minus signs above and below.
  • Winter vs. summer: A smaller mirrored building shows the reversed flow in a hot, air-conditioned summer.
  • Fire inset: A floor-plan view of a smoke plume drawn toward a stairwell, then a second panel with a pressurized stair preventing it.
  • Consequences: Three callouts: door that slams or will not open, whistling at the elevator lobby, uneven heating between floors.
  • Beau: Warning pose.

docs.title: Poster 14: The Swiss Cheese Model of Building Failure
docs.text:
Influence: James Reason's Swiss cheese model (1990), which shows that accidents happen when holes in several layers of defense line up. It is widely used in safety engineering, healthcare, and aviation. This poster applies it to buildings, which is a teaching adaptation rather than a published building standard.

Core message: Buildings rarely fail from one cause. Failure happens when holes in several defenses line up.

Chapters: 17, 18, 21

Image description:

  • Layout: Five upright slices of Swiss cheese seen in perspective, with a single orange arrow passing through aligned holes from left to right.
  • Slices, left to right: Design (a code-compliant but unbuildable detail), Materials (substituted product), Construction (a missed flashing), Inspection (skipped or rushed), Maintenance (clogged gutter, ignored leak).
  • End result: A building icon with a damaged corner, with the label "Mold, collapse, or fire spread."
  • Example case strip: Three real failure types shown generically, such as a roof leak, a deck collapse, and a smoke-spread incident, each with its aligned holes.
  • Fix panel: A second set of slices with fewer, offset holes, labeled "Redundancy."
  • Beau: Encouraging pose with a hard hat and a clipboard.

docs.title: Poster 15: The Living Building Petals
docs.text:
Influence: The International Living Future Institute's Living Building Challenge, built from seven performance areas, or "petals": Place, Water, Energy, Health and Happiness, Materials, Equity, and Beauty, with 20 imperatives in all (ten core and ten that push performance further).

Core message: A building can give more than it takes: it can generate energy, treat water, and improve its place.

Chapters: 20

Image description:

  • Layout: A large flower with seven petals around a building at the center.
  • Petal contents: Place (a walkable, restored site), Water (a rain cistern and green roof), Energy (solar panels), Health and Happiness (a daylit room), Materials (a non-toxic, transparent materials list), Equity (people of all abilities and incomes sharing a common space), Beauty (a sculptural detail and a mural).
  • Center: A building icon labeled "Living Building."
  • Contrast strip: Along the bottom, a "less bad" building versus a "net positive" building, with arrows showing resources in and out.
  • Beau: Celebration pose.

docs.title: Poster 16: Nature in the Room
docs.text:
Influence: Terrapin Bright Green's 14 Patterns of Biophilic Design, published in 2014. A tenth-anniversary edition adds a fifteenth pattern, Awe. The patterns fall into three groups: Nature in the Space, Natural Analogues, and Nature of the Space.

Core message: Daylight, views, and natural materials are not decoration; they are inputs to occupant health.

Chapters: 4, 16

Image description:

  • Layout: A single richly drawn interior (a classroom or office) in the center, with callout lines to features.
  • Three color-coded groups: Nature in the Space (plants, water feature, daylight, breezes), Natural Analogues (wood grain, biomorphic forms, material patterns), Nature of the Space (a prospect view, a sheltered refuge nook, a path that reveals more).
  • Lighting link: A daylight-versus-electric-light strip that ties to the lighting systems in Chapter 16.
  • Footer: "Design for the human body, not just the code."
  • Beau: Neutral pose, relaxed, near a window.

docs.title: Poster 17: When the Power Goes Out
docs.text:
Influence: Alex Wilson coined passive survivability in 2005, after Hurricane Katrina, for a building's ability to maintain critical life-support conditions during an extended loss of power, heating fuel, or water. The Resilient Design Institute argues it should be a baseline for residential codes.

Core message: A good building keeps its occupants safe even when the grid and the furnace fail.

Chapters: 19, 21

Image description:

  • Layout: A two-panel before/after of the same Minnesota house in a January blackout.
  • Panel A, Typical house: Thin insulation, leaky envelope, dark windows. A thermometer inside drops quickly from 68 °F toward freezing, with a clock ticking.
  • Panel B, Resilient house: A well-insulated, airtight envelope with a south-facing window letting in low winter sun, and a thermometer that holds a safer temperature much longer.
  • Strategy ring: Icons for insulation, air sealing, passive solar gain, daylighting, natural ventilation, and shading.
  • Question strip: "How many hours until it is unsafe?" with a student-fillable blank that can later become a MicroSim input.
  • Beau: Tip pose with a blanket and a flashlight.

docs.title: Poster 18: Minnesota Asks Hard Questions
docs.text:
Influence: U.S. climate-zone classification, in which Minneapolis falls in zone 6A (cold-humid) and northern Minnesota in zone 7, together with the Minnesota Energy Code. The course description emphasizes frost-protected foundations, high-performance insulation, air sealing, and ice-dam and moisture control. Pull any numeric requirements directly from the current adopted code; do not copy values from secondary summaries.

Core message: Climate is the first design input. Each system in a Minnesota building has a cold-climate answer.

Chapters: 9, 10, 11, 13

Image description:

  • Layout: A Minnesota state outline in the center with the 6A and 7 zones shaded, with a house cross-section on the right.
  • Questions and answers: Five "hard question" callouts from the climate, each with a matched design answer on the house. Frost depth (deep or frost-protected footings), freeze-thaw (durable concrete and drainage), long heating season (heavy insulation and air sealing), ice dams (roof air sealing and ventilation), summer humidity (dehumidification and moisture control).
  • Climate data strip: Design-temperature and degree-day figures, to be filled from an authoritative source such as ASHRAE or the code itself.
  • Beau: Warning pose in a parka and hard hat.

docs.title: Poster 19: Idea to Occupancy
docs.text:
Influence: The integrated team process in the WBDG and the standard phases of the design and construction process: programming, schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding, construction, commissioning, and occupancy.

Core message: A building is created by a sequence of people and decisions, and the earlier a decision is made, the cheaper it is to get right.

Chapters: 2, 16, 17

Image description:

  • Layout: A winding road from the left (idea) to the right (occupancy), with eight milestone signs.
  • Swim lanes: Under the road, horizontal bars show who is most active in each phase: owner, architect, structural engineer, mechanical engineer, electrical designer, contractor, code official and inspector.
  • Influence curve: An overlaid curve showing that the ability to influence cost and performance is highest at the start, with a falling cost-of-change line crossing a rising effort line. Draw this as a conceptual curve, not a data plot.
  • Electrical designer highlight: A callout marks where electrical design coordinates with the other trades, which supports Dunwoody's electrical-design audience.
  • Beau: Welcome pose at the start of the road.

docs.title: Poster 20: The Building Systems Map
docs.text:
Influence: Research on holistic synergy analysis of building subsystems, together with the systems thinking that runs through Building America, Passive House, and the WBDG. Treat this as the capstone poster that ties the course together.

Core message: Every system depends on every other. Change one and the others must respond.

Chapters: 14, 15, 16, 19

Image description:

  • Layout: A network diagram with seven large nodes arranged in a ring: Structure, Enclosure, HVAC, Plumbing, Electrical, Fire Protection, Occupants.
  • Links: Labeled arrows connect the nodes. Examples: Enclosure to HVAC, a tighter envelope shrinks the heating load and requires mechanical ventilation. HVAC to Electrical, heat pumps raise the electrical service demand. Structure to Fire Protection, the structural material sets the fire-resistance rating and the sprinkler needs. Plumbing to Enclosure, pipes in exterior walls risk freezing and leaks. Occupants to everything, behavior drives load and wear.
  • Ripple example: A highlighted pathway shows one change (adding triple-pane windows) rippling through to a smaller heating system, a smaller electrical service, and lower cost, with an opposing arrow noting added cost and weight.
  • Link density: Line thickness shows how strongly two systems interact.
  • Footer: "No system is an island."
  • Beau: Celebration pose, since this poster summarizes the whole book.

docs.title: Suggested Production Order
docs.text:
1. Posters 1, 2, 3, 7, 20: the five most holistic. They frame the whole book.
  2. Posters 4, 5, 6, 10: the core physics posters, tied to Chapters 3 to 6.
  3. Posters 8, 11, 12, 15: the sustainability and performance cluster.
  4. Posters 9, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19: the cross-cutting and applied posters.

docs.title: Sources Consulted
docs.text:
These are the sources behind the framework summaries above. I read search-result summaries and, for Architecture 2030, the page text. I did not view the original artwork.

  • BSI-001: The Perfect Wall, Building Science Corporation
  • BSI-120: Understanding Walls, Building Science Corporation
  • BSI-075: How Do Buildings Stack Up?, Building Science Corporation
  • Shearing layers and How Buildings Learn, Wikipedia
  • Building America: Managing the Drivers of Air Flow and Water Vapor Transport, U.S. Department of Energy
  • Building Science Introduction: Moisture Flow, PNNL
  • Whole Building Design, Whole Building Design Guide
  • How to Design a Passive House: The 5 Core Principles, Passive House Accelerator
  • The National Human Activity Pattern Survey (NHAPS), Klepeis et al.; and We Spend 90% of Our Time Indoors. Says Who?, BuildingGreen
  • Harvard Healthy Buildings Program: Homes for Health
  • Climate, Comfort and Natural Ventilation: A New Adaptive Comfort Standard for ASHRAE Standard 55, de Dear and Brager
  • Why the Built Environment, Architecture 2030

docs.title: The Carbon Footprint of the Built World
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a region and read what it counts and which source it comes from. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the region it describes.

The poster keeps two accountings in separate regions. The three warm-toned regions on the left are Architecture 2030's numbers. The blue region on the upper right is UNEP and GlobalABC's numbers. The seven regions are:

  1. Built Environment Share (Architecture 2030) — About 42% of annual global CO2 emissions, pulled out of the whole.
  2. Operational Carbon (Architecture 2030) — About 27% from running buildings.
  3. Embodied Carbon (Architecture 2030) — About 15% more from materials and construction.
  4. UNEP GlobalABC Accounting — 32% of global energy and 34% of global CO2, on a different boundary.
  5. Materials Behind Embodied Carbon — Cement, steel, aluminum, timber, glass, and insulation.
  6. New Floor Area, 2020 to 2060 — About 2.6 trillion square feet (241 billion square meters) still to be built.
  7. Different Boundaries, Different Numbers — Why two sources can both be right.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Two respected sources give two different shares for the built world's carbon footprint. Architecture 2030 reports about 42% of annual global CO2 emissions (about 27% operations plus about 15% embodied carbon). The UNEP and GlobalABC 2024/2025 report gives 32% of global energy and 34% of global CO2. The numbers differ because the sources count different things with different methods, so this poster never mixes them in one number. When you quote a share, name the source and what it includes.

The lesson holds under either accounting: buildings are a leading climate lever, and as operating energy falls, materials account for a growing share of the total. Percentages here are as published at the time of writing and are updated by their sources; check the current pages before citing them.

  • UNEP and GlobalABC. Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2024/2025, and the GlobalABC publication page. Source of the 32% energy and 34% CO2 figures.
  • RICS. Whole life carbon assessment for the built environment. Source of the cited UNEP estimate of about 28% operational and 12% embodied for 2021.

docs.title: Cradle to Grave to Cradle
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a region and read what each life-cycle module covers. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the region it describes.

The nine regions, from the building's start to its end and then the carbon brackets:

  1. Product Stage (A1 to A3) — Extracting, hauling, and manufacturing the materials.
  2. Transport and Construction (A4 to A5) — Delivery to the site and the building process.
  3. Use Stage: Upkeep and Replacement (B1 to B5) — Repairs, replacements, and refurbishment.
  4. Use Stage: Energy and Water (B6 to B7) — The energy and water the building uses.
  5. End of Life (C1 to C4) — Demolition, waste handling, and disposal.
  6. Module D: Beyond the Boundary — The potential benefit of reuse and recycling.
  7. Embodied Carbon: Making, Building, and Upkeep — The material-related modules through the use stage.
  8. Operational Carbon: Energy and Water — Only the energy and water modules.
  9. Embodied Carbon: End of Life — The end-of-life modules, which are also embodied.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Building life-cycle assessment sorts a building's impacts into labeled modules, following the European standard EN 15978: A for the product and construction stages, B for the use stage, C for end of life, and D for benefits beyond the boundary. Chapter 20 introduces the same labels. RICS's whole life carbon standard classes modules A through C, except B6 and B7, as embodied carbon, and B6 and B7 as operational carbon.

The poster uses the common module set. RICS's 2023 edition adds a pre-construction module A0 (assumed to be zero for buildings) and a user-carbon module B8, which are left out here. Module D is reported separately and is only a potential benefit.

docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

The eight callouts are:

  2. Continuous Super-Insulation
  3. High-Performance Windows and Doors

  5. Airtight Construction
  6. Balanced Ventilation with Heat Recovery
  7. Thermal-Bridge-Free Design
  8. The Result: Energy Savings

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Passive House is a voluntary, performance-based building standard from the Passive House Institute. It rests on five principles: very good thermal insulation, highly efficient windows, controlled ventilation with heat recovery, no thermal bridges, and airtightness. Chapter 19 treats it as one of the demanding targets that go beyond the code minimum.

The poster draws the five principles in one cutaway house so students can see why they belong together. The star diagram is a teaching device and not part of the standard. The energy-savings figure is the Institute's own claim. It is stated against typical existing building stock, so it is not a promise for any single project. The exact criteria, such as heating demand and airtightness targets, are set by the standard and the climate, so check them with a certified designer.

docs.title: Four Ways Moisture Moves
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what drives that pathway and how to control it. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The five regions are:

  1. Bulk Water — Liquid water from rain, snowmelt, groundwater, or a leak, driven by gravity and wind pressure.
  2. Capillary Action — Water drawn through tiny pores by surface tension, even upward.
  3. Air-Transported Moisture — Vapor carried by air leaking through gaps wherever there is a pressure difference.
  4. Vapor Diffusion — Vapor moving through solid materials from the humid side to the dry side.
  5. Damage Potential Ranking — A schematic comparison of how much harm each pathway can do.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Building scientists separate moisture into four transport mechanisms because each one needs a different control: flashing and drainage for bulk water, capillary breaks for wicking, an air barrier for air-carried vapor, and drying capacity for diffusion. A designer who controls only one leaves the other three working. The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's Building America materials call bulk moisture the most damaging mechanism, and Building America research finds that airflow typically carries an order of magnitude or more water vapor than diffusion does.

The ranking bars are schematic. The sources agree on the two ends of the ranking, but none publishes a single numeric scale for all four mechanisms, so the poster shows order and not measured quantities.

Building America Partnership for Improved Residential Construction, revised October 2012. Source for airflow carrying one or more orders of magnitude more water vapor than diffusion.
  • Building Science Corporation. BSD-106: Understanding Vapor Barriers. Background on air-carried vapor.

docs.title: Heat on the Move
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read how that kind of heat flow works and where it shows up in a building. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The six regions are:

  1. Conduction — Heat passing through a solid by molecular collisions.
  2. Convection — Heat carried by moving air or water.
  3. Radiation — Heat travelling as electromagnetic waves, with no material needed.
  4. Thermal Bridges — Framing and other paths that carry heat around the insulation.
  5. Slab Without a Thermal Break — A concrete balcony slab that runs unbroken through the wall.
  6. Slab With a Thermal Break — The same balcony with an insulating layer interrupting the slab.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Conduction, convection, and radiation are the standard textbook description of how heat moves, and building science adds the practical consequence: heat takes the easiest path, so an R-value printed on insulation describes the insulation alone and not the whole wall. Studs, slab edges, and gaps let heat go around it. Passive House practice makes thermal-bridge-free detailing one of its five core principles for that reason.

The thermal image is a teaching illustration drawn from the physics described in Chapter 3, not a real scan, and the balcony details are simplified. Actual performance depends on the product, the climate, and the detailing, so use the adopted energy code and the manufacturer's data for real projects.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
The U.S. Department of Energy's Building America program states the idea this way: the total performance of a house depends on a balance of the envelope, the mechanical systems, and the occupants, and all three affect the flow of heat, air, and moisture into and out of the house. The poster turns that statement into a picture. Each marker belongs to one of the three actors, and each acts on the same three flows.

The scene is a teaching illustration, not a product diagram. Real houses differ by climate, age, and equipment, and the details shown, such as a heat-recovery ventilator in the attic, are examples rather than requirements. The point is the interaction: change one part, and the others respond.

docs.title: Idea to Occupancy
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a phase and read what happens, who is most active, and where the electrical designer and the code official come in. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the phase it describes.

The eight phases, in order:

  1. Programming — The owner's needs, budget, and schedule are written down.
  2. Schematic Design — The architect explores the overall form and layout.
  3. Design Development — The systems are chosen and sized.
  4. Construction Documents — The final drawings and specifications are produced and reviewed for the permit.
  5. Bidding and Procurement — The owner chooses the builder and secures materials.
  6. Construction — The work is built, observed, and inspected.
  7. Commissioning — The installed systems are tested against the design intent.
  8. Occupancy and Closeout — The building is inspected, certified, and handed over.

The poster also sketches two conceptual ideas. The colored lanes show which roles are most active in each phase, and two curves show that the ability to influence cost and performance falls while the cost of a change rises. Neither is a data plot.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
This poster is a composite of standard concepts. It uses the eight phases that Chapter 2 of this book uses, the electrical designer's coordination role from Chapter 16, and the permit, plan review, and inspection steps from Chapter 17. It is inspired by the integrated team process described by the Whole Building Design Guide, but it is not a published diagram.

The swim lanes and the two curves are conceptual. They show relative emphasis and direction, not measured effort or dollar amounts, and real projects overlap phases and vary by delivery method. The lesson holds anyway: early decisions are made on paper, when a change costs an hour, and late changes are made in finished work.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
The International Living Future Institute (ILFI) built its Living Building Challenge around seven performance areas, called petals: Place, Water, Energy, Health and Happiness, Materials, Equity, and Beauty. The program has 20 imperatives, ten core and ten that push performance further, and it judges a project on measured results after 12 months of occupancy rather than on design intent. Its central idea is regeneration: a building should give back, not only take less.

Most of this book teaches how to reduce harm, which is the "less bad" side of the contrast strip. The petals show where that work is heading. Each petal here is a simplified summary in general terms, so read ILFI's current standard before claiming that any project meets a specific requirement.

docs.title: Minnesota Asks Hard Questions
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a region and read the climate question and its design answer. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the region it describes.

The seven regions are:

  1. Minnesota Climate Zones — Minneapolis is in zone 6A and northern Minnesota in zone 7.
  2. Climate Data to Look Up — Design temperatures and degree days come from published data, not memory.
  3. Ice Dams — Seal the ceiling, insulate, then ventilate the roof.
  4. Long Heating Season — A continuous, airtight, well-insulated wall with warm-side vapor control.
  5. Frost Depth — Footings below the frozen zone, or frost-protected foundations.
  6. Freeze-Thaw — Air-entrained concrete, durable masonry, and drainage.
  7. Summer Humidity — Dehumidification, sealed and insulated surfaces, and a drying path.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
U.S. climate zones sort places by temperature and moisture so that one set of code tables can serve a whole region. Minnesota spans two of them: zone 6A for most of the state, including Minneapolis, and zone 7 for the northern counties. Because climate fixes what the weather will do to a building, it is the first design input, and each hard question here has a design answer drawn from Chapters 9, 10, 11, and 13.

The poster deliberately prints no energy-code numbers. Insulation values, window ratings, air-leakage limits, and design temperatures depend on the edition of the code in force, so read them from the adopted Minnesota Energy Code and the local building official. Zone assignments are summarized from a Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry code-change proposal and should be confirmed against the adopted rules.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
In 2014 Terrapin Bright Green published 14 Patterns of Biophilic Design, which sorts the ways people connect with nature in buildings into three groups: Nature in the Space, Natural Analogues, and Nature of the Space. A tenth-anniversary edition adds a fifteenth pattern, Awe. The poster shows nine of the fourteen original patterns: Visual Connection with Nature, Dynamic and Diffuse Light, Thermal and Airflow Variability, Presence of Water, Material Connection with Nature, Biomorphic Forms and Patterns, Prospect, Refuge, and Mystery. Five others, including Complexity and Order, are not drawn.

The patterns are a design framework, not a code requirement, and the strength of the evidence behind each one varies. The lighting strip is this book's own link to Chapters 16 and 19: daylight pays off only when the controls respond.

docs.title: The Six S's of Shearing Layers
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a layer and read how long it lasts and what it contains. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the layer it describes.

The six layers, from slowest to fastest:

  1. Site — The land, soil, climate, and legal lot, effectively eternal.
  2. Structure — The foundation and load-bearing frame, roughly 30 to 300 years.
  3. Skin — The exterior surfaces, roughly 20 years.
  4. Services — Wiring, plumbing, ducts, and sprinklers, roughly 7 to 15 years.
  5. Space Plan — Interior partitions and layout, roughly 3 to 30 years.
  6. Stuff — Furniture and belongings, changing daily.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
The lifespans come from Stewart Brand's How Buildings Learn (1994), which expanded Frank Duffy's earlier layered model into six layers. Brand's point is that a building is always being pulled apart by components that age at different rates. A building that lets those layers slip past one another can adapt; one that locks them together has to be torn down.

Lifespans are Brand's rules of thumb, not code requirements. Real buildings vary with climate, use, and maintenance.

docs.title: The Swiss Cheese Model of Building Failure
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a region and read what it contributes to a failure. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the region it describes.

The eight regions, from the first defense to the fix:

  1. Design Slice — Drawings and details that are both compliant and buildable.
  2. Materials Slice — The right products, delivered in good condition.
  3. Construction Slice — Work built as designed.
  4. Inspection Slice — Checks that catch what earlier slices missed.
  5. Maintenance Slice — Upkeep for the whole life of the building.
  6. Failure Outcome — What the arrow does when the holes align.
  7. Three Generic Failure Chains — A roof leak, a deck collapse, and a smoke-spread incident.
  8. Redundancy and Offset Holes — Independent defenses that do not line up.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
James Reason, then at the University of Manchester, published the Swiss cheese model in 1990 to explain accidents in complex systems. Each layer of defense has holes, and an accident happens when the holes in several layers line up. Safety engineering, aviation, and healthcare use the model widely.

This poster applies it to buildings. That application is a teaching adaptation, not a published building standard, and the five slices (design, materials, construction, inspection, maintenance) are a choice made for this book. The failure examples are generic composites, not real events. Chapter 21 teaches the same lesson in its failure chains, and Chapter 18 uses the same picture for fire protection layers.

docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over a numbered marker or its label and read what it shows. Use Quiz mode to read the name in the prompt, then click the marker that matches. The marker numbers are hidden, so you must find the matching part of the picture.

The ten callouts are:

  1. Elevator Shaft and Stairwell as Flues
  2. Warm Air Escapes High
  3. Uneven Heating Between Floors
  4. Summer Reverses the Flow
  5. Smoke Drawn Toward the Stairwell
  6. Cold Air Enters Low
  7. Doors That Slam or Stick
  8. Whistling at the Elevator Lobby
  9. Neutral Pressure Plane

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
The stack effect is the vertical air movement caused by the difference in density between warm indoor air and cold outdoor air. Building Science Corporation's BSI-075 describes it: in winter air leaves a heated building through the top and enters through the bottom, with a neutral pressure plane between them, and the flow reverses in cooling seasons. The effect grows with building height and temperature difference.

The same pressure that wastes heat and causes drafts can compromise smoke control in tall buildings, which is why fire engineers care. The smoke panels are a teaching simplification: real smoke movement also depends on the fire's own heat, the building's leaks, and its smoke-control design, which engineers analyze for each building.

The map's seven nodes are Structure, Enclosure, HVAC, Plumbing, Electrical, Fire Protection, and Occupants. docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
This poster is a teaching synthesis, not a published diagram. It draws on the "house as a system" framing used by the U.S. Department of Energy's Building America program, in which the envelope, the mechanical systems, and the occupants together determine performance. It also draws on research into holistic synergy analysis of building subsystems by Lumpkin, Horton, and Sinfield (2020).

Every relationship shown is a standard building-science link covered in Chapters 14, 15, 16, and 19. The ripple example shows how to follow one change through the systems, including the push-back from added cost, weight, and unchanged ventilation load. Real buildings have more links than seven nodes can show.

docs.title: The Indoor Species
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a region and read what it covers. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the region it describes.

The ten regions, the clock ring first and then the nine foundations, are:

  1. Where the Day Goes — How the day is divided between indoors, vehicles, and outdoors.
  2. Ventilation — Enough outdoor air to dilute odors, chemicals, and carbon dioxide.
  3. Air Quality — Low-emission materials and removal of pollutant sources.
  4. Thermal Health — Comfortable, steady temperature and humidity with individual control.
  5. Moisture — Inspecting for and fixing leaks, condensation, and damp spots.
  6. Dust & Pests — Cleaning and sealing so allergens and pests do not settle in.
  7. Safety & Security — Fire safety, carbon monoxide monitoring, and emergency preparedness.
  8. Water Quality — Safe drinking water, tested at the point of use.
  9. Noise — Protection from outdoor sound and control of mechanical noise.
  10. Lighting & Views — Daylight, task lighting, and sightlines to the outdoors.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
The "90% indoors" figure traces to the National Human Activity Pattern Survey (NHAPS), funded by the U.S. EPA and reported by Klepeis and colleagues (2001). Its respondents, surveyed by telephone diary in 1992 to 1994, spent about 86.9% of their time indoors and about 5.5% in vehicles. That is an average of surveyed U.S. respondents, not a universal constant, so treat it as a strong rule of thumb.

The nine foundations come from the Healthy Buildings program at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. The poster pairs the two ideas: if people live indoors, the building is their habitat. The clock ring is an illustration of the survey averages, and the foundation summaries are paraphrased from Harvard.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Structural engineers teach that every load must have a continuous path to the ground, and that each link must be strong enough, stiff enough, and connected to the next. The poster follows one orange route from the roof to the soil, then shows three ways the route breaks: a missing uplift tie, a removed bearing wall, and a footing on soft ground.

This poster is a composite of standard structural concepts, not a single published diagram. It is simplified: real houses carry loads through many parallel paths, and gravity, wind, and earthquake loads each need their own. Use it to learn the habit of tracing a load, and rely on the adopted code and a licensed engineer for any real design or remodel.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
In Building Science Corporation's BSI-001, Joseph Lstiburek describes a wall that controls rain, air, vapor, and heat, with all four control layers placed outside the structure. From the outside in the order is cladding, drainage space, water control, air control, vapor control, thermal insulation, structure, and interior finish. The priority is rain, then air, then vapor, then thermal, and each lower priority is wasted if the one above it fails.

The poster draws the layers separately so they are easy to count. Real walls often combine layers in one material. Real walls also vary by climate, so check the adopted code and an enclosure designer before copying any assembly.

docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
P. O. Fanger's Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) model, the standard method in ASHRAE Standard 55, predicts how a large group will vote on a seven-point sensation scale from six variables: air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air speed, and humidity (environmental), plus clothing insulation and metabolic rate (personal). Brager and de Dear's adaptive model adds that, in occupant-controlled spaces without mechanical cooling, acceptable indoor temperatures also move with the outdoor climate.

The three case scenes are teaching examples, not measurements. Chapter 4 gives a rough winter comfort range, but no numeric range is stated here because ranges depend on the standard's edition, humidity, and the occupants. Check the current edition of ASHRAE 55 before design.
